passage:
At nine, Jasleen read aloud slowly, stumbling over long words, and her classmates waited. That evening she pushed her book away. "I'm dumb," she said. "I can't read." The next day she stopped raising her hand at all. Her father Ojas sat beside her and asked, "Which words tripped you?" There were only four, and they practised them until bedtime. The label "dumb" shrank to four hard words.

At fifteen, Jasleen was going to interview for a summer job at the library. Her heart hammered, her hands felt cold and she couldn't sit still. "I'm terrified," she told her friend Rafiq. He tilted his head. "You've got the same racing heart as before your trip to the hills. That was excitement." She thought about it, took a breath and said aloud, "I'm excited. I'm nervous, but I'm ready."

Her heart was still racing as she walked into the interview, but now it had a different name.

qa.q: How many words tripped Jasleen when she read aloud at nine?
How do the names Jasleen gives herself at nine and at fifteen show the effect of labels?
qa.a: At nine the label "dumb" makes her stop trying, until Ojas turns it into four hard words she can practise; at fifteen she renames a racing heart from terrified to excited and nervous but ready, so the label shapes what she does next.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she told Rafiq she was terrified?
qa.a: Jasleen was anxious and afraid, with her heart hammering and her hands cold, although the same body signals could also mean excitement.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that helped Jasleen at nine?
qa.a: He asked which words tripped her and practised the four hard ones with her, replacing a vague label with a skill that could be practised.

grounding: Labelling: a child's label of dumb that stops effort, and a teenager who names mixed eager and worried feelings as excitement to feel ready.
